If you see gaps, prototype HG-RAG by integrating a hierarchical knowledge graph (e.g., using Neo4j or a simple tree structure) and implement the three-step retrieval: anchor entity resolution, then upward/lateral/downward traversal.
whatToTry.note: Start with a small domain (e.g., 100-200 nodes) to test the approach before scaling. The paper's code is not yet released, but the algorithm is straightforward to implement.

items.title: Hybrid Models Beat Scale: Access Structure Key to AI Capability
items.tldr: A new paper proposes the Capability Convergence Hypothesis (CCH), showing that under fixed inference budgets, AI capability depends on access structure (compressive state + verbatim index) rather than scale. Pre-registered tests confirm a 'scissors gap' where hybrid models drastically outperform pure state or attention-only architectures on tasks requiring both retrieval and reasoning.
whyItMatters: For founders building AI products: This suggests that hybrid architectures (e.g., combining state-space models with attention) can achieve higher capability per compute than scaling up monolithic models, enabling more efficient and cost-effective AI systems.

Technically, it identifies three resource walls (Shannon, horizon, circuit) that pure architectures hit, but hybrids can cross, guiding architecture choices for long-context or retrieval-heavy applications.

whatToTry.description: Evaluate your current model architecture for tasks requiring both exact retrieval (e.g., from a knowledge base) and reasoning. Consider prototyping a hybrid model that pairs a compressive state (like an RNN or state-space model) with a global attention layer, as the paper shows this combination can achieve near-perfect retrieval accuracy where pure models fail.
whatToTry.note: Start with small-scale tests on your specific use case (e.g., document QA or code generation) to see if the 'scissors gap' applies, before committing to full-scale training.

For example, when a search agent ignores a new API, provide a context like 'What if you had used the new search tool instead?' to break inertia.

whatToTry.description: If you're building a RAG system over structured knowledge (e.g., a knowledge graph or hierarchical database), prototype a simple graph-traversal step: after entity extraction from a query, expand context by fetching parent, sibling, and child nodes before passing to the LLM. Start with a small graph (under 1000 nodes) to test improvements on multi-hop queries.
whatToTry.note: This works best when your data has explicit hierarchical relationships (e.g., categories, org structures). For flat document stores, consider adding metadata tags to simulate hierarchy.

items.title: New Test Reveals LLMs' 'Right Answer, Wrong Reasoning' in Chain-of-Thought
items.tldr: A new black-box audit method (interventional grounding audits) detects when LLM chain-of-thought reasoning doesn't genuinely depend on its premises, finding that 66% of correctly solved problems have flawed reasoning. This is critical for building trustworthy AI products.
whyItMatters: For AI product builders: This method provides a practical way to audit your LLM's reasoning fidelity, catching 'right answer, wrong reasoning' issues that undermine trust in applications like legal, medical, or financial advice.
Technically: It offers a step-level, black-box test that outperforms self-consistency baselines (F1 0.806 vs 0.343), enabling better evaluation of CoT reliability without needing model internals.

whatToTry.description: Implement interventional grounding audits in your evaluation pipeline: for each premise in a CoT output, substitute a key predicate with a novel symbol (e.g., 'is_a' -> 'is_b'), re-run the model, and check if the conclusion changes. If not, the reasoning may be spurious. Use the provided GitHub repo for reproduction scripts.
whatToTry.note: Start with formal, parsable benchmarks like ProntoQA; the method's scope is limited outside such structured domains.

whatToTry.description: Review the survey's taxonomy of update targets (model parameters vs. scaffold components) and signals (e.g., reward, human feedback, self-supervised). whatToTry.description: If you're building multi-agent systems, experiment with bridge-seeking routing: instead of connecting agents with similar outputs (threshold-similarity), deliberately route messages between agents with high disagreement to prevent fragmentation and improve consensus.

items.title: Prompt Formatting Can Flip AI Benchmarks: New Study
items.tldr: A new study shows that minor formatting changes in prompts can alter model accuracy by over 30x, potentially flipping leaderboard rankings. This is crucial for founders building AI products that rely on consistent, parseable outputs.
whyItMatters: Business impact: Your AI product's reliability may be fragile to prompt formatting changes, affecting user trust and output consistency.
Technical impact: Benchmarking without controlling for prompt wrappers is statistically fragile; you need to test multiple formats to get a true measure of model performance.

whatToTry.description: When evaluating models for your product, test each candidate with at least 3 different prompt wrappers (e.g., different delimiters, instruction placements) and track both accuracy and parseability. Use the Format Sensitivity Index (FSI) and Parseability Sensitivity Index (PSI) as metrics to select models that are robust to formatting changes.
whatToTry.note: Focus on models with low FSI and PSI for structured-output tasks like JSON generation or API calls.

items.title: LLM Agent Relays: Structured Messages Work for Strong Models
items.tldr: New research reveals that in multi-hop agent relays, structured message formats (JSON, triples) don't degrade accuracy for strong LLMs, but for weak models they cause a 8.7x wider recall spread. This challenges the 'telephone game' assumption and offers practical guidance for agent pipeline design.
whyItMatters: For founders building multi-agent systems: strong models (e.g., GPT-4 class) can use structured formats without fidelity loss, enabling cost savings from shorter messages.
For teams using smaller models: format choice becomes critical—JSON with fixed keys resists drift better than free text, but rigid formats incur an encoding toll.

whatToTry.description: If your agent relay uses a strong model (e.g., GPT-4), switch to JSON or key-value formats to cut token costs without harming accuracy. For weak models, test both JSON with a fixed schema and free text with precision instructions to find the best trade-off for your specific hop count.
whatToTry.note: The study used 6 hops; test with your actual relay depth to confirm effects.

sources.title: Faithful, Not Corrective: Message-Format Effects in Multi-Hop Agent Relays Are Tier-Dependent

items.title: YUKTI: Robust Decision-Making with Uncertainty-Typed Propositions

This matters for founders building AI that allocates real resources, as it directly addresses fragility in current LLM-based optimization pipelines.
whyItMatters: Business impact: Enables AI systems to make safer, auditable decisions in regulated domains like healthcare, finance, and logistics, reducing risk of costly failures from overconfident point estimates.
Technical impact: Provides a principled method to handle uncertainty in autoformulation, with proven regret bounds and traceability, potentially becoming a new standard for robust AI planning.

whatToTry.description: Review your current AI decision pipeline for reliance on single-point objective coefficients. Consider integrating uncertainty quantification (e.g., distributional Pareto hand-offs) and resampling assumptions to test robustness, especially for high-stakes allocations.
whatToTry.note: Start with a small-scale pilot on a non-critical decision to evaluate the overhead of multi-stage solvers and ARPF before full adoption.

items.title: Execution-Gated Self-Distillation Boosts Code Gen 5x
items.tldr: A new paper shows that using a deterministic, ungameable filter (whether generated code launches cleanly) for rejection-sampling self-distillation dramatically improves code generation quality, raising clean generation from 8.8% to 42.2% on unseen game families. This is a practical method for improving AI code generators without learned judges.
whyItMatters: Business impact: Founders building AI code generation tools can use this execution-gated approach to significantly boost model performance on complex, multi-file projects without expensive human feedback or learned reward models.

Technical impact: Demonstrates that a simple, deterministic filter (strict-launch) is more effective than learned judges for self-improvement, and that verifier precision is critical—lenient filters erase gains entirely.

whatToTry.description: Implement a deterministic execution gate for your code generation pipeline: after generating a project, run it in a headless environment (e.g., headless Godot for games, or a sandboxed server for web apps) and only keep generations that launch cleanly. Use these successful samples to fine-tune your model via rejection-sampling self-distillation, iterating over multiple rounds.
whatToTry.note: Ensure the filter is strict and ungameable—avoid lenient checks like BUILD-only, as they provide no signal. Start with a small model (e.g., 14B) and LoRA to keep costs low.
